summary: East end of Long Point, Lake Erie: first lit in 1830, rebuilt in concrete in 1916 as the third light on the site, automated in 1989.

structures.note: Third light on the site; 1,700 ft south-east of its predecessor (LighthouseFriends).
Second light on the site, 60 ft high in 1876 (LighthouseFriends).
First light on the site; contract specified a stone tower of fifty feet; taken down 1838 or 1839 (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Owned by the Canadian Coast Guard. Best viewed by boat; summer boat tours to the tip have been offered (LighthouseFriends).

visit.tours: Summer boat tours to the tip have been offered (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Stone tower first lit on the evening of 3 November 1830; finished the following summer (LighthouseFriends).
First tower taken down, 1838 or 1839, as erosion undermined it; moved inland (LighthouseFriends).
Second tower, wood and octagonal, built near the tip (LighthouseFriends).
Steam foghorn in service on 1 May 1892 (LighthouseFriends).
New keeper's house, coal shed, barn and boathouse (Department report).
New fog alarm building housing a diaphone run by an oil engine (LighthouseFriends).
Present concrete octagonal tower, third on the site, by Charles Mattaini for $8,490 (LighthouseFriends); the heritage statement gives the Department of Marine and the 1916 date.
Radiobeacon began operation, call sign VGF (LighthouseFriends).
Bird kill at the tower in early September; keeper Lorne Brown reported it to William E. Saunders (LighthouseFriends, summarising Saunders in The Auk, 1930).
Barge Mary McLaughlin, total wreck, 7 July 1913; crew of five rescued by the Long Point life-saving crew.
Steamer C. W. Elphicke ashore off the point, 21 October 1913; crew of 18 rescued by the life-saving crew.
Long Point life-saving crew went to the steamer W. H. Stevens of Buffalo burned at Clear Creek, 7 September 1902; her crew had landed in their own boats (a separate establishment from the light).
Much of the point became the Long Point National Wildlife Area (LighthouseFriends).
Long Point designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve (LighthouseFriends).
Heritage character statement, dated 18 June 1987, gives the tower a Recognized designation (FHBRO Building Report 86-77).
Light automated; third-order lens replaced by a solar-powered beacon (LighthouseFriends).
Third-order Fresnel lens removed on automation; later displayed at Port Burwell Marine Museum (LighthouseFriends).

wrecks.outcome: Barge; total wreck. Crew of five rescued by the Long Point life-saving crew.
Steamer ashore off Long Point. Crew of 18 rescued by the life-saving crew after a long pull.
Steamer of Buffalo burned at Clear Creek. Her crew had landed in their own boats before the Long Point crew arrived.

notes_for_editor: 1) Keepers 1830-1989 come from LighthouseFriends alone. Department keeper lists confirm only Sheldon B. Cook (1906, 1907): the OCR splits name and station into separate columns, so other names were not matched by position. Check the page images for Price through Clarke, Woodward, Stalker, Brown, Ansley and Nelder before publishing. 2) First light (3 Nov 1830) and the 1829 contract are LighthouseFriends' figures, which cite the Board of Works reports; those reports are not in the corpus. The contract sum is shown with a damaged currency sign on LighthouseFriends, so it is left out. 3) The 1828 Whittlesey letter is quoted through LighthouseFriends; the original was not read. 4) The 1929 bird-kill figures come from LighthouseFriends' summary of W. E. Saunders, The Auk 47 (1930): 507-511. JSTOR returned only a stub and OUP refused access; verify before publishing. 5) The Long Point life-saving station (near Port Rowan, 1902) is a separate establishment and may need its own record; its rescues appear here only as events and wrecks with that note. 6) The W. H. Stevens burning is placed at Clear Creek only. Clear Creek's location relative to the light is not given in our sources, so the event is not claimed as a light-station wreck. 7) The west-end light (Long Point Cut, 1879-1919) is a separate station; its own record should carry it. 8) The 1987 heritage date is the statement's own date (1987.06.18); no designation date was found. 9) Post-1960 keepers (Ansley, Nelder) and Brown's bird-kill work are recorded in role only; no personal detail was added. 10) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1913-14 permanent-crew line is the Long Point entry (Point Pelee has its own identical line, which the story does not use). The 1902 W. H. Stevens paragraph sits in the Long Point station write-up (scan 37, printed p. 24). The 1879 west-end light is described in the 1879 Department notice quoted by LighthouseFriends; the story says described in 1879, not built. The 1914-1928 keeper gap is LighthouseFriends' own list. Cook is matched on OCR lines with the station name in the 1906 and 1907 keeper lists; those page images were not viewed. The 1828 letter is still read through LighthouseFriends, as footnote 2 states.
